hints: Look at the sign of $\Delta H_{2} = +27.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ in Table 2.1 and think about whether products finish higher or lower in energy than reactants.
Recall the definitions: $E_{A}$ is measured from reactants up to the top of the hump, while $\Delta H$ is measured from reactants to products.
walkthrough:
Use the sign of delta H to place products**
Think of $\Delta H$ as products minus reactants. Here $\Delta H_{2} = +27.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, so products contain more energy than reactants. Draw a curve that starts at the $\text{NaHCO}_{3} + \text{HCl}$ line, goes up over a hump, then levels off at $\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$ clearly above the starting level.

Add the two labelled arrows**
Picture the journey. $E_{A}$ is the initial push needed to reach the top, so draw an upward arrow from the reactant line to the very top of the hump. $\Delta H_{2}$ is the overall change, so draw a separate arrow from the reactant line to the product line and label it $+27.2 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: Curve starting at $\text{NaHCO}_{3} + \text{HCl}$, rising to a hump then falling to $\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$ at a higher level than reactants (endothermic profile).
$E_{A}$ arrow from reactant level to top of hump. $\Delta H_{2}$ arrow from reactant level to product level, labelled +27.2.

hints: The equation produces $\text{CO}_{2}$ gas, so think about what you would see while gas is evolving and what changes when it stops.
walkthrough:
Link the equation to what you see**
Both reactions make $\text{CO}_{2}$ gas: $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-} + 2\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$. In the cup this appears as fizzing or effervescence. While solid is disappearing you also see bubbles. When all the carbonate has reacted no more gas can form, so the fizzing stops and the solution goes still.
Final answer: Effervescence / fizzing stops, no more bubbles of $\text{CO}_{2}$ evolved.

hints: Start with heat gained by the solution using $Q = mc\Delta T$, taking $m = 50.0 \text{ g}$ and $\Delta T = 26.2 - 19.6$.
Convert $Q$ to $\text{kJ}$ and divide by the moles of $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$ reacted (0.0400 mol) to get energy per mole.
Decide the sign of $\Delta H_{1}$ by checking whether temperature rose or fell, remembering that heat released by reaction gives negative $\Delta H$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the heat taken in by the solution**
Treat the $50.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$ of solution as $50.0 \text{ g}$ with $c = 4.18 \text{ J g}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$. Temperature rises, so the solution gained heat: $$Q = mc\Delta T = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times (26.2 - 19.6)$$ $$Q = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times 6.6 = 1379.4 \text{ J} \approx 1.38 \text{ kJ}$$

Scale to one mole of reaction**
That heat came from $0.0400 \text{ mol}$ of $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$ reacting as in reaction 1. Energy per mole: $$\frac{1.3794 \text{ kJ}}{0.0400 \text{ mol}} = 34.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Apply the correct sign and units**
Temperature went up, so the reaction released heat. It is exothermic, so $\Delta H$ must be negative: $$\Delta H_{1} = -34.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Always give $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and a negative sign for an observed temperature rise.

Final answer: $Q = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times (26.2 - 19.6) = 1379 \text{ J} = 1.38 \text{ kJ}$
$\Delta H_{1} = -Q / 0.0400 = -34.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (exothermic).

hints: Write out $2 \times$ (reaction 2) and compare with reaction 1 plus reaction 3 to see how they combine to give $2\text{NaHCO}_{3} \rightarrow \text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$.
Remember to multiply $\Delta H_{2}$ by 2 because two moles of $\text{NaHCO}_{3}$ are needed, and to subtract $\Delta H_{1}$ with careful handling of its negative sign.
walkthrough:
Build a Hess route to reaction 3**
You want: $2\text{NaHCO}_{3} \rightarrow \text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$. If you take $2 \times$ reaction 2 you get $2\text{NaHCO}_{3} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} + 2\text{CO}_{2}$. Then subtract reaction 1 ($\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$) and the $2\text{HCl}$, $2\text{NaCl}$ and extra $\text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$ cancel to leave exactly reaction 3.

Combine the enthalpy values**
By Hess's law: $$\Delta H_{r} = 2\Delta H_{2} - \Delta H_{1}$$ Substitute your numbers: $$\Delta H_{r} = 2(27.2) - (-34.5) = 54.4 + 34.5 = +88.9 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The double negative becomes addition, giving a strongly endothermic decomposition, as expected for heating a hydrogencarbonate.
Final answer: $\Delta H_{r} = 2\Delta H_{2} - \Delta H_{1} = 2(27.2) - (-34.5) = +88.9 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

hints: Identify the Period 4 Group 2 metal and write the formula of its nitrate, remembering nitrate is $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$.
Recall the general Group 2 nitrate decomposition to metal oxide plus $\text{NO}_{2}$ (brown) plus $\text{O}_{2}$, then balance the equation.
walkthrough:
Identify Z from the clues**
Period 4 Group 2 is calcium, $\text{Ca}$. A nitrate contains $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$, so with $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ you need two nitrates: $\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_{3})_{2}$. The brown gas on heating is the classic test for a nitrate decomposing to give $\text{NO}_{2}$.

Write the balanced decomposition**
All Group 2 nitrates (except the special case) decompose on heating: metal nitrate to metal oxide + nitrogen dioxide + oxygen. For calcium: $$\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_{3})_{2} \rightarrow \text{CaO} + 2\text{NO}_{2} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2}$$ Check atoms: $\text{Ca}$ 1 each side, $\text{N}$ 2 each side, $\text{O}$ 6 on left and $1 + 4 + 1 = 6$ on right.
